passage: My name is Amandeep, and this is about the week I did not paint. On Monday I decided to become a painter, so I drew a timetable with six colours of pen. On Tuesday I bought brushes and a tube of every colour with my pocket money. On Wednesday I covered the timetable in stickers. By Saturday I had a beautiful chart and a box of new paints, and my friend Thomas asked, "Can I see your first painting?" I opened the sketchbook and looked at the clean white pages. There was nothing on them. I had spent a whole week getting ready to start, and I had mistaken that for starting.

qa.q: How many colours of pen did Amandeep use for the timetable?
qa.a: Amandeep used six colours of pen.

qa.q: What did Amandeep feel when Thomas asked to see a painting?
qa.a: Caught out and a little embarrassed, since there was nothing on the pages after a week of preparing. 😅

qa.q: What could Amandeep do first to actually start?
qa.a: Paint something small for ten minutes today, even if it is messy, because doing it beats more planning.

qa.q: How might Thomas see that week?
qa.a: As all preparation and no painting, though Thomas asked kindly and simply wanted to see a first attempt.

grounding: Amandeep spends a week on a colourful timetable and new supplies but never paints, mistaking planning for progress.

passage:
Note for Keerthana's parents, art club, Friday
Keerthana joined painting club on Monday, full of plans. On Monday she drew a timetable in six colours: painting Monday to Saturday, 4 to 5 pm, with a sun sticker for each day. On Tuesday she asked for a list of supplies, and by Wednesday she had a new palette, twelve brushes and a smock. On Thursday she redid the timetable because the first one "looked messy". Today she arranged her brushes by size for most of the hour. Not one painting yet. When I asked, she said, "I'm almost ready." I have asked her to paint anything at all, even a single leaf, on Monday before she touches the timetable. Could you ask her at home what she wants to paint first?
— Vandana, art club

qa.q: How many brushes did Keerthana have by Wednesday?
qa.a: She had twelve brushes, along with a new palette and a smock.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling when she said she was almost ready?
qa.a: She may have felt excited about painting but nervous about a messy first picture, so getting ready felt safer than starting.

qa.q: What would you change first for Keerthana?
qa.a: Paint first and plan later: one small painting on Monday, even a single leaf, would turn a week of preparation into real progress.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Keerthana's week?
qa.a: Vandana sees plenty of energy going into timetables and supplies but no painting, and asks the parents to help nudge Keerthana to start.

grounding: An art club note shows a child spending a week on a colourful timetable and supplies but never actually painting.

passage:
Saturday
Dear diary, this was supposed to be my painting week. Monday I made the timetable: blue for sky practice, green for trees, red for FREE PAINTING. Tuesday Rekha Didi took me to the stationery shop for poster colours and a thick pad. Wednesday I made a better timetable with a ruler. Thursday I sorted the colours in rainbow order and labelled the jars. Friday was the last day to hand in a picture for the school competition. I hadn't done one. I told Miss Joseph I was "still planning". Today Rekha Didi asked to see my paintings. I showed her the timetable. She didn't laugh, but she didn't say anything either. The pad is still white. I feel a bit silly.
Eshaan

qa.q: What did Eshaan do on Thursday?
qa.a: Eshaan sorted the colours in rainbow order and labelled the jars.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when Rekha Didi asked to see the paintings?
qa.a: Eshaan felt embarrassed and silly, having only a timetable and a white pad to show after a whole week.

qa.q: What else could Eshaan have done on Monday?
qa.a: Paint one quick picture before making any timetable, so there would have been something to hand in for the competition on Friday.

qa.q: What might Rekha Didi's silence mean?
qa.a: She may have been surprised or a little disappointed, but kind enough not to laugh, perhaps leaving Eshaan room to notice the gap.

grounding: A child's diary shows a week of timetables and supplies with no painting, and the missed competition that followed.
